items.title: Plain English: rewriting drafts (Level 3)
items.source: GOV.UK Style Guide; GOV.UK content design guidance
items.body: Rewriting a weak draft is a core skill. Start by asking what the reader needs to know and do, then cut everything else. Common problems to look for are passive sentences that hide who is acting, long sentences with several ideas, vague requests, padding words, and abstract nouns formed from verbs. For example, 'The carrying out of an assessment will take place' is better as 'We will assess your claim'. Turn passive sentences into active ones: 'Your application was rejected by the committee' becomes 'The committee rejected your application'. Make requests specific. 'Send us more information soon' does not say what or when, whereas 'Send us your latest payslip by Friday 14 March' does. Where you have bad news, give an alternative if there is one: 'You can apply online or by post' is more helpful than 'You cannot apply by phone'. Cut hedging when you are sure. If someone is entitled to a refund, say 'You are entitled to a refund', not 'You may possibly be entitled'. Use 'must' for something that is a requirement and avoid 'should' where you mean a rule. Replace 'e.g.' and 'i.e.' with 'for example' or 'that is'. Finally, check that your rewrite still means exactly the same thing. Plain English should never change the facts or promise more than the department can deliver.

questions.prompt: Which is the best rewrite of 'Your application was rejected by the committee because the form was not signed'?

options.text: The committee rejected your application because you did not sign the form.
Your application has been rejected as a result of the unsigned form.
The form was not signed, so your application was rejected by the committee.
Rejection of your application occurred because the form was unsigned by you.

questions.hint: The active version puts the doer first and says who did what.

questions.prompt: Which is the plainest version of 'It would be appreciated if you could possibly let us know whether or not you will be able to attend'?

options.text: We would appreciate knowing about your possible attendance.
Kindly advise us as to whether you will be in attendance.
Please tell us if you can attend.
Please let us know whether or not you will be able to attend.

questions.hint: Cutting padding leaves the request short and clear.

questions.prompt: What is the main problem with: 'Claimants who wish to apply for the benefit in question are required to submit the relevant documentation to the address below prior to the closing date'?

options.text: It is written in the first person and sounds too personal for a government letter
It uses distant, formal wording instead of speaking to the reader and naming the documents
It leaves out the address so that people cannot reply to the department
It contains a Latin abbreviation that many readers will not know

questions.hint: The draft should say 'you', name the documents and give the date.

questions.prompt: What is the main problem with: 'Your claim, which was received on 2 May and which we have reviewed, cannot be paid because the evidence, which you sent late, was incomplete.'?

options.text: It is too short to explain the reason for the decision
It is written entirely in the passive voice, so nobody is named
Too many ideas are packed into one long sentence
It does not mention the claim or the date it was received

questions.hint: Splitting it into several short sentences would make it easier to follow.

questions.prompt: Which rewrite fixes the vagueness in 'Send us more information soon'?

options.text: Send us your latest payslip by Friday 14 March.
Send us the information we asked for at your earliest convenience.
Send us any other information that may be useful as soon as you can.
Send us more details about your situation within a reasonable time.

questions.hint: A good request names what is needed and when.

questions.prompt: Which is the more helpful way to say 'You cannot apply by phone'?

options.text: You can apply online or by post.
Phone applications are not accepted by this office.
We do not offer a telephone application service.
Applying by phone is not possible at present.

questions.hint: Telling readers what they can do is more helpful than only saying what they cannot.

questions.prompt: Which sentence follows GOV.UK style?

options.text: Bring documents e.g. a passport or driving licence.
Bring documents, i.e. a passport or driving licence.
Bring documents such as a passport or driving licence.
Bring documents (passport, driving licence, etc.).

questions.hint: Plain 'such as' or 'for example' replaces Latin abbreviations.

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly shows that something is a legal requirement?

options.text: You might want to tell us about any change of address.
You are advised to tell us about any change of address.
You must tell us about any change of address.
You should tell us about any change of address.

questions.hint: 'Must' is used for obligations; 'should' sounds optional.

questions.prompt: Which sentence avoids unnecessary hedging, when the refund is certain?

options.text: We believe you might qualify for a refund of £45.
It seems you could be entitled to a refund of £45.
You may possibly be entitled to a refund of £45.
You are entitled to a refund of £45.

questions.hint: If the fact is certain, say it directly.

questions.prompt: Which sentence avoids the heavy noun 'the carrying out of an assessment'?

options.text: An assessment of your claim will be carried out.
Your claim will be subject to assessment.
We will assess your claim.
The carrying out of an assessment will happen.

questions.hint: Turning a noun back into a verb makes the sentence shorter and active.

items.title: Plain English: tone and knowing your reader (Level 3)
items.source: GOV.UK Style Guide; GOV.UK content design guidance
items.body: Before you write, think about who will read your message and what they need. A person writing about a stopped payment may be worried about paying rent, so they want to know what has happened, what you are doing and when it will be fixed. Start with the reader's need, not the department's process. Avoid idioms and figures of speech such as 'touch base', 'ballpark figure' or 'end of play', because they confuse readers whose first language is not English and sound like jargon to everyone. Avoid sarcasm and jokes, because tone is hard to judge in writing. Do not blame the reader. Say 'We did not receive your form' instead of 'You failed to return your form'. Show empathy in a straightforward way, such as 'I understand this is worrying', and then give facts. Do not offer false comfort such as 'Don't worry, everything will be fine' if you do not know that it will. If you must use a technical term that the reader needs, use it and explain it the first time, for example 'your National Insurance number (the number on your NI card)'. Finish by telling people how to get help, such as the number to call and the days and hours it is open. To test your writing, ask a colleague who does not know the case to read it and tell you what they think they must do.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is least likely to confuse a reader whose first language is not English?

options.text: We will contact you by Friday.
We will circle back to you before the week wraps up.
We will touch base with you before the week is out.
We will get back to you by the end of play on Friday.

questions.hint: Plain, literal language is easier for everyone to understand.

questions.prompt: Which sentence avoids blaming the reader?

options.text: We did not receive the form. Please send it again.
You failed to return the form.
You neglected to send the form on time.
The form was not returned by you.

questions.hint: Describing what happened without accusing the reader keeps the tone helpful.

questions.prompt: Why should you avoid sarcasm in written messages?

options.text: Sarcasm is only a problem in emails
The reader cannot hear your tone and may take it seriously
Sarcasm is banned by the Civil Service Code
Sarcasm makes sentences longer

questions.hint: Written tone is easily misread.

questions.prompt: What should you think about first before writing a message?

options.text: How long the message should be, to fit the page
Who will read it and what they need to know or do
Which font and layout to use for the final version
Who else in the department should see a copy first

questions.hint: Starting with the reader shapes everything else.

questions.prompt: A technical term cannot be avoided because the reader needs it. What should you do?

options.text: Use it without explanation, as readers will look it up
Use it and explain it the first time
Replace it with a different, unrelated word
Put the explanation at the end of the letter in a footnote

questions.hint: Explaining a necessary term when first used helps readers.

questions.prompt: Which sentence shows empathy without making a promise the department cannot keep?

options.text: There is really nothing at all for you to be concerned about.
I understand this is worrying, and I will explain what happens next.
I'm sure you'll be very pleased with the final outcome here.
Please don't worry, because everything will be fine in the end, I promise.

questions.hint: Empathy plus facts is better than false reassurance.

questions.prompt: Which closing line is the most helpful?

options.text: Do not hesitate to contact us should you require further clarification.
Please feel free to reach out at any time if needed.
We trust that this letter has clarified the position.
If you have a question, call us on the number above, Monday to Friday.

questions.hint: A helpful closing says how and when to get help.

questions.prompt: What is a good way to test whether your message is clear?

options.text: Read it through again yourself straight after finishing it
Run a spell check and a grammar check on the whole text
Check that it is under the word count your team normally uses
Ask someone who does not know the case what they think they must do

questions.hint: A fresh reader finds problems you cannot see.

questions.prompt: Why does a figure of speech such as 'ballpark figure' cause problems?

options.text: It is only used for money
It always makes a sentence too long
It is illegal in official letters
Some readers will not understand it

questions.hint: Idioms may mean nothing to readers who are not familiar with them.

items.title: Writing for web pages and documents (Level 3)
items.source: GOV.UK Style Guide; GOV.UK content design guidance
items.body: Many people read government information on a phone, so GOV.UK prefers web pages to PDFs. A web page works on any screen size and with a screen reader, while a PDF can be hard to read on a phone. Write headings that tell people what is in each section and put the important words first, such as 'Apply for a passport'. Use a clear page title, and keep headings in order, with a main heading followed by smaller ones. Use the word 'select' instead of 'click', as people may use a mouse, keyboard, touch screen or voice. Do not write 'see above' or 'see below', because the layout of a page changes between devices. Link to the page by its name instead. Link text should make sense alone, because screen reader users often hear a list of links. Use a table only for data in rows and columns, not for layout. Introduce a bulleted list with a lead-in line ending with a colon, and start each bullet with a lower-case letter unless it is a proper noun. If you must produce a document file, give it a clear name using lower-case letters and hyphens, such as 'housing-claim-form-2025.docx'. Include the date or version where it helps readers to tell versions apart.

questions.prompt: Which verb does GOV.UK style prefer for telling users to press a button or link?

options.text: Tap
Hit
Select
Click on

questions.hint: 'Select' works whatever device the person is using.

questions.prompt: Why does GOV.UK prefer web pages to PDFs?

options.text: Web pages work better on phones and with screen readers
PDFs are not allowed to be used anywhere in government departments
Web pages are much cheaper to print than other formats
PDFs cannot be saved onto a computer or a mobile phone

questions.hint: HTML pages adapt to different screens and assistive technology.

questions.prompt: Why should you avoid writing 'see below' on a web page?

options.text: Screen readers do not read the word 'below'
It makes sentences longer
It is the wrong spelling
The layout changes on different devices, so 'below' may be wrong

questions.hint: Web page layouts differ between phones and computers.

questions.prompt: Which heading is most helpful?

options.text: Section 3
Additional information
Further details relating to the matter
Apply for a passport

questions.hint: A good heading puts the important words first.

questions.prompt: Why must link text make sense on its own?

options.text: Links are not allowed in the middle of sentences
Links are always printed in a table
Search engines ignore the rest of the sentence
Screen reader users often hear links read out as a list

questions.hint: Meaningful link text helps people who navigate by links.

questions.prompt: When is it right to use a table?

options.text: When showing data in rows and columns
When adding a decorative border
When arranging the page into two columns
When you need to make text smaller

questions.hint: Tables are for data, not for layout.

questions.prompt: Which file name follows the recommended style?

options.text: housing claim form new.docx
housing-claim-form-2025.docx
Housing Claim Form (FINAL v3).docx
HOUSING_CLAIM_FORM_2025.DOCX

questions.hint: Lower-case letters and hyphens are tidy and web-friendly.

questions.prompt: How should a lead-in line for a bulleted list end?

options.text: With a full stop, and each bullet is a complete sentence
With no punctuation, and each bullet starts a new topic
With a colon, and each bullet then reads on from it
With a question mark, and each bullet answers it

questions.hint: A colon links the lead-in to the points that follow.

questions.prompt: Why include a date or version in a file name where it helps?

options.text: Readers can tell different versions apart
The file cannot be changed after it is saved
The file opens much faster on older computers
The file size is smaller once the date is added

questions.hint: Dates and versions prevent people using out-of-date forms.

items.title: Emails: replying, copying people in and signatures (Level 3)
items.source: GOV.UK content design guidance; Civil Service Code
items.body: Use Cc only for people who need to be aware of the message but do not have to act. Copying in too many people fills inboxes and hides who is responsible for the action. If you reply to a large group, check whether everyone needs your answer before you press 'Reply all'. A simple 'thanks' sent to 200 people creates 200 unnecessary emails. If a customer's query belongs to another team, tell the customer who will deal with it and by when, and copy in the colleague with a short note so that the customer does not have to explain again. Use 'Forward' to pass a message on to someone who was not in the original email, and add a line saying what you need them to do. A professional email signature should include your name, job title, team or department and a contact number or address. Do not add your personal mobile number unless your department allows it, and keep logos and images small. Make the next step clear in the closing line. 'I will update you by Friday 14 March' is better than 'More information will follow in due course'. If you ask for something, say who should do it and by when. Check the whole email chain before you forward it, because earlier messages may contain information the new reader should not see.

questions.prompt: When is it right to put someone in the Cc field?

options.text: When you are unsure who the real recipient is
When you want their reply to be private
When they need to be aware of the message but not act on it
When they must reply with a decision

questions.hint: Cc is for information only.

questions.prompt: A colleague replies all to a 200-person email with the single word 'Thanks'. What is the problem?

options.text: It tells the sender that the message was not read
It breaks the confidentiality of the original email chain
It fills 200 inboxes with a message most people do not need
It removes other people from the mailing list by mistake

questions.hint: Unnecessary reply-all messages waste time.

questions.prompt: A customer's query belongs to another team. What is the best response?

options.text: Ignore it until the other team contacts them
Ask the customer to send the query again to the right team
Tell the customer who will deal with it and by when, and copy in that colleague
Delete it and ask the other team to reply

questions.hint: This saves the customer from repeating themselves.

questions.prompt: Which items belong in an email signature?

options.text: Name, job title, team and contact number
A long legal quotation and your date of birth
Your home address and a personal photograph
Your whole career history and qualifications

questions.hint: A signature gives the reader the details needed to contact you.

questions.prompt: Which closing line makes the next step clearest?

options.text: More information will follow in due course.
I will update you by Friday 14 March.
I will get back to you at some point.
We will be in touch if anything changes.

questions.hint: A date makes the next step concrete.

questions.prompt: Why should you add a line when forwarding an email to a colleague?

options.text: To confirm that the original email has been read
To change the subject of the whole email chain
To tell them what you need them to do
To hide the earlier messages from the new reader

questions.hint: Forwarded messages should state the action required.

questions.prompt: What is a risk of forwarding a long email chain without checking it?

options.text: The subject line will be lost
The original sender will be notified
Older messages may contain information the new reader should not see
The chain may become too large to be forwarded

questions.hint: Earlier parts of a chain may include personal data or comments.

questions.prompt: Why should logos and images in a signature be small?

options.text: Small images are easier to print
Images are banned in government email
Large images cannot be sent outside the department
Large images make emails heavy and can appear as unwanted attachments

questions.hint: Heavy signatures slow down messages and clutter replies.

items.title: Answering a member of the public (Level 3)
items.source: Civil Service Code; ICO guidance; Equality Act 2010
items.body: When a member of the public contacts you, work out what they need before you answer. Listen or read carefully and, if you are unsure, ask a question. Before you discuss personal information, check that you are speaking to the right person by asking the security questions your department uses. Do not give out information to a third party, such as a relative, unless the person has given permission or the third party has legal authority. You can say that you are unable to discuss the case and explain how the person can give permission. If you do not know the answer, say so, find out and tell them when you will reply. Do not guess. Do not give legal or financial advice beyond your role. Instead, signpost the person to the right service or GOV.UK page. The Equality Act 2010 requires organisations to make reasonable adjustments for disabled people, such as large print or extra time. Use an approved interpreter service if the person needs one, rather than relying on a family member. If a person is angry, stay calm, let them finish, acknowledge how they feel and focus on what you can do. Never make promises you cannot keep. If they want to make a complaint, explain how, and do not take it personally. Record the contact accurately, so the next person does not have to ask the same questions.

questions.prompt: A caller asks about their mother's claim and has no written permission. What should you do?

options.text: Give general details only, without mentioning any amounts
Confirm only whether a claim exists for her at all
Ask them to prove they are related by giving their own address
Explain you cannot discuss it without her permission and say how it can be given

questions.hint: Personal information is shared with a third party only with authority.

questions.prompt: You do not know the answer to a customer's question. What is the best response?

options.text: Give your best guess to avoid delay
Say you will find out and tell them when you will reply
Tell them to contact another department without checking
Say the question cannot be answered

questions.hint: Honesty and a follow-up date keep trust.

questions.prompt: Why do you check identity before discussing a case?

options.text: To record how many callers each day are customers
To make sure the customer is a resident of the UK
To increase the length of the call for the records
To avoid disclosing personal information to the wrong person

questions.hint: Identity checks protect personal data.

questions.prompt: Which is an example of a reasonable adjustment under the Equality Act 2010?

options.text: Providing a letter in large print for someone with sight loss
Offering a shorter appointment time to anyone who has a disability
Asking the person to bring a friend to read it to them
Sending the same letter to everyone to keep things fair

questions.hint: Reasonable adjustments help disabled people access services.

questions.prompt: A caller asks for advice on whether to take legal action against a landlord. What is best?

options.text: Tell them what you would do if you were in their position
Explain you cannot give legal advice and signpost to a suitable service
Give your opinion based on your own experience of similar cases
Suggest that the case is probably not worth pursuing at all

questions.hint: Staff should not give advice outside their role.

questions.prompt: A caller is angry and shouting. Which approach is best?

options.text: Match their tone so that they know you are serious
Say clearly that the problem is not your fault
Tell them you will end the call if they carry on
Stay calm and acknowledge how they feel

questions.hint: Calm listening usually reduces anger.

questions.prompt: A customer needs an interpreter. What should you do?

options.text: Use an approved interpreter service
Reply in simple English and repeat it slowly
Ask them to bring a friend next time
Ask a family member to translate for them

questions.hint: Approved interpreters are impartial and reliable.

questions.prompt: Why should you record each contact accurately?

options.text: So the call can be shortened the next time they ring
So the next person does not have to ask the same questions
So that the customer can listen to it afterwards
So the call can be used as evidence against the customer

questions.hint: Good records help continuity.

items.title: Letters to the public: layout, wording and addressing (Level 3)
items.source: GOV.UK content design guidance; ICO guidance
items.body: Small details in a letter affect how it is received. Put a short heading at the top that states the subject, such as 'Your claim for Housing Benefit: decision', so the reader knows immediately what the letter is about. Many letters carry two references: 'Our ref' is the number your department uses, and 'Your ref' is the number the customer quoted, if they gave one. If you do not know someone's title, or do not want to guess it, GOV.UK guidance suggests using their full name, such as 'Dear Aisha Khan', rather than assuming 'Mr' or 'Ms'. Check that the name and address match your records, and be especially careful with a letter that contains personal data. A wrong address can be a data breach. If a letter holds sensitive information, mark it 'Private and confidential' so that the envelope is opened only by the person it is for. Check that the personal data inside a window envelope cannot be seen through the window, other than the name and address. Use short paragraphs and break long letters into sections with headings. Put the key date and the action in the first paragraph, and number the pages as 'Page 1 of 2' for longer letters. Sign the letter, or mark where it has been signed on your behalf, and give your name and job title underneath so the reader knows who wrote it.

questions.prompt: What does 'Your ref' at the top of a letter show?

options.text: The reference number of the person who wrote the letter
The reference number the customer quoted
The number of pages in the letter
The reference number of the department's file

questions.hint: 'Your ref' is the customer's own reference.

questions.prompt: Why include a short heading that states the subject of the letter?

options.text: So the sender can avoid using a reference
So the letter fits neatly on to one page
So the letter can be filed in the right place
So the reader knows immediately what it is about

questions.hint: A heading orients the reader.

questions.prompt: You do not know whether a customer prefers Mr, Ms or Mx. What does GOV.UK guidance suggest for the greeting?

options.text: Use 'Dear Mr' to be safe, then follow up
Use their full name, such as 'Dear Aisha Khan'
Use 'Dear Customer' followed by their reference number
Use 'Dear Sir or Madam' for every such letter

questions.hint: A full name avoids assuming a title.

questions.prompt: What is the risk of putting the wrong address on a letter that contains personal data?

options.text: The customer will have to pay for postage
It can be a data breach
The letter will lose its reference number
The letter will be returned unopened

questions.hint: Sending personal data to the wrong person is a breach.

questions.prompt: When should you mark a letter 'Private and confidential'?

options.text: When it is addressed to a business
When it is a routine acknowledgement
When it contains an enclosure
When it contains sensitive information for the named person only

questions.hint: The marking protects the contents from other people at the address.

questions.prompt: What should you check about a window envelope?

options.text: That the stamp is next to the window
That the letter is folded in three
That only the name and address can be seen through the window
That the window is the correct shape

questions.hint: Other personal data must not show through.

questions.prompt: Where should the key date and required action go in a letter?

options.text: In the final paragraph
In the middle of the second page
In a postscript
In the first paragraph

questions.hint: The reader should see the most important facts first.

questions.prompt: Why give your name and job title under the signature?

options.text: So the reader knows who wrote to them
So the reader can complain about you
So the letter can be filed under your name
So that the letter looks longer and more formal

questions.hint: Giving your name and role makes the letter accountable and helpful.

items.title: Spreadsheets: the IF function (Level 3)
items.source: Microsoft Excel help; Google Sheets help
items.body: The IF function makes a decision. Its form is =IF(test, value_if_true, value_if_false). The test is a comparison, and the spreadsheet returns the second part if the test is true, and the third part if not. Comparison operators are = (equal to), <> (not equal to), > (greater than), < (less than), >= (greater than or equal to) and <= (less than or equal to). Text in a formula must be in double quotation marks, such as "Pass". Suppose A2 holds 65. Then =IF(A2>=50,"Pass","Fail") returns Pass. If A2 holds 50, it still returns Pass because >= includes 50, but =IF(A2>50,"Pass","Fail") would return Fail. Text comparisons are not case sensitive, so "yes" equals "Yes". You can place one IF inside another, called nesting, to handle more than two outcomes. For example =IF(A2<0,"Negative",IF(A2=0,"Zero","Positive")) returns Zero when A2 holds 0. AND and OR combine tests. AND returns true only if all tests are true, and OR returns true if at least one is. For example =IF(AND(A2>=18,B2="UK"),"Eligible","Check") returns Eligible only when both conditions are met. If you leave out the false part, IF returns FALSE when the test is not met. Always check every case, including values at the boundary such as exactly 50.

questions.prompt: With 65 in A2, which result comes back from =IF(A2>=50,"Pass","Fail")?

options.text: Pass
Fail
TRUE

questions.hint: 65 is greater than 50, so the test is true.

questions.prompt: Cell A2 now holds exactly 50. What is returned by the >= version of the Pass or Fail formula?

options.text: FALSE
Pass
Fail

questions.hint: >= includes the boundary value 50.

questions.prompt: Cell A2 holds exactly 50. What is returned if the test is changed to A2>50?

options.text: Pass
Fail
TRUE

questions.hint: 50 is not greater than 50, so the false result is returned.

questions.prompt: Which operator means 'not equal to'?
questions.hint: <> is the 'not equal to' operator.

questions.prompt: Why are quotation marks used around Pass in an IF formula?

options.text: To tell the spreadsheet to ignore the word
Text in a formula must be in double quotation marks
To make the cell show the word in a bold font
To make the result of the formula a number

questions.hint: Without quotes the spreadsheet looks for a name.

questions.prompt: B2 holds yes in lower case. What does =IF(B2="Yes","Send","Hold") return?

options.text: Send
#VALUE!
FALSE
Hold

questions.hint: Text comparisons in spreadsheets are not case sensitive.

questions.prompt: A2 holds 0. What does =IF(A2<0,"Negative",IF(A2=0,"Zero","Positive")) return?

options.text: Negative
Positive
Zero

questions.hint: The first test fails and the second is true.

questions.prompt: A2 holds 20 and B2 holds UK. What does =IF(AND(A2>=18,B2="UK"),"Eligible","Check") return?

options.text: UK only
Eligible
TRUE
Check

questions.hint: Both conditions are true, so AND is true.

questions.prompt: A2 holds 5. What does =IF(A2>10,"High") return?

options.text: Zero
FALSE
High
Low

questions.hint: When the false part is left out, IF returns FALSE.

items.title: Spreadsheets: COUNTIF, SUMIF and AVERAGEIF (Level 3)
items.source: Microsoft Excel help; Google Sheets help
items.body: COUNTIF, SUMIF and AVERAGEIF do a calculation only on cells that meet a condition. The form is =COUNTIF(range, criteria), =SUMIF(range, criteria, sum_range) and =AVERAGEIF(range, criteria, average_range). Imagine a table with departments in A2:A7 and spending in B2:B7. A2:A7 holds HR, Finance, HR, IT, Finance and HR. B2:B7 holds 100, 250, 150, 300, 50 and 200. Then =COUNTIF(A2:A7,"HR") returns 3, because HR appears three times. =SUMIF(A2:A7,"HR",B2:B7) adds the amounts on the rows where the department is HR, so it returns 450. =AVERAGEIF(A2:A7,"HR",B2:B7) returns 150. =SUMIF(A2:A7,"Finance",B2:B7) returns 300. Criteria can be a number comparison in quotation marks. =COUNTIF(B2:B7,">100") counts the amounts above 100, so it returns 4. =SUMIF(B2:B7,">=200") adds amounts of 200 or more, and returns 750 because only 250, 300 and 200 qualify. =COUNTIF(A2:A7,"<>HR") counts the cells that are not HR and returns 3. Criteria for text are not case sensitive. The range and the sum range must be the same size, or the answer will be wrong. If no cell meets the condition, COUNTIF returns 0 and SUMIF returns 0, but AVERAGEIF returns the error #DIV/0!.

questions.prompt: Using A2:A7 (HR, Finance, HR, IT, Finance, HR), how many cells does =COUNTIF(A2:A7,"HR") count?
questions.hint: HR appears on three rows.

questions.prompt: What total comes from adding the amounts on the HR rows with SUMIF?
What is the mean spend of the HR rows when AVERAGEIF is used?
questions.hint: 450 divided by 3 is 150.

questions.prompt: How much do the two Finance rows come to when added using SUMIF?
How many cells in B2:B7 (100, 250, 150, 300, 50, 200) does =COUNTIF(B2:B7,">100") count?
questions.hint: Amounts above 100 are 250, 150, 300 and 200.

questions.prompt: What does =SUMIF(B2:B7,">=200") return for 100, 250, 150, 300, 50 and 200?
What does =COUNTIF(A2:A7,"<>HR") return?
questions.hint: Finance, IT and Finance are not HR.

questions.prompt: What happens if no cells meet the condition in an AVERAGEIF formula?

options.text: It returns 0

items.title: Spreadsheets: relative and absolute references (Level 3)
items.source: Microsoft Excel help; Google Sheets help
items.body: A reference in a formula can be relative or absolute. A relative reference, such as A1, changes when you copy the formula to another cell. An absolute reference has dollar signs, such as $A$1, and does not change. The dollar sign locks the column letter, the row number, or both. In Excel for Windows you can press F4 while editing a formula to add the dollar signs. A mixed reference locks only one part, so $A1 locks the column and A$1 locks the row. Absolute references matter when one cell holds a value that many formulas use, such as a VAT rate in B1. A formula =B4*B1 copied down from row 4 to row 5 becomes =B5*B2, which points to the wrong cell. Using =B4*$B$1 copied down two rows becomes =B6*$B$1, which keeps the rate cell fixed. Copying =A1+B1 from C1 across to D1 gives =B1+C1, because relative references move one column to the right. Mixed references help in tables such as multiplication grids. If =$A2*B$1 is copied one column right and one row down, it becomes =$A3*C$1. Remember that copying and pasting a formula adjusts relative references, but cutting and pasting a formula moves it and keeps the references the same.

questions.prompt: What does a dollar sign in a reference such as $A$1 do?

options.text: Turns the number into a currency
Makes the cell read-only
Marks the cell as containing money
Locks the column and row so they do not change when copied

questions.hint: The dollar sign makes the reference absolute.

questions.prompt: Which key adds dollar signs to a reference when editing a formula in Excel for Windows?

options.text: F4
F7
F2

questions.hint: F4 cycles through the types of reference.

questions.hint: The relative part moves two rows and the absolute part stays.

questions.hint: Both relative references move down one row.

questions.hint: $B$1 stays fixed in every copy.

options.text: The column only
Neither
The row only
The row and column

questions.hint: The dollar sign sits before the column letter, so only the column is locked.

questions.prompt: =A1+B1 sits in C1 and is copied across to D1. What does it become?
questions.hint: Relative references move one column to the right.

options.text: They become errors
They stay the same
They become absolute
They all move by the same amount

questions.hint: Cutting moves a formula, so references do not adjust.

items.title: Spreadsheets: averages, ranges and simple charts (Level 3)
items.source: Microsoft Excel help; Google Sheets help
items.body: Three averages describe data in different ways. The mean is the total divided by the number of values. The median is the middle value when the numbers are in order. The mode is the value that appears most often. The range is the difference between the largest and smallest values. For the numbers 3, 5, 5, 8 and 14, the mean is 7 because the total is 35 and there are five values. The median is 5, the mode is 5 and the range is 11 because 14 minus 3 is 11. With an even number of values, the median is the mean of the two middle values: for 2, 4, 6 and 10 it is 5. Spreadsheets have the functions MEDIAN, MODE and AVERAGE for these. The median is useful when a few very large values would make the mean misleading. Charts help readers to see patterns. A bar or column chart compares amounts across categories, such as calls handled by each team. A line chart shows change over time, such as applications per month. A pie chart shows how a whole is divided and works best with a few slices. Every chart needs a clear title, labelled axes and units. A chart can mislead if the vertical axis does not start at zero, because small differences look large.

questions.prompt: A team handled 3, 5, 5, 8 and 14 cases on five days. What is the mean per day?
questions.hint: The total is 35 and 35 divided by 5 is 7.

questions.hint: The middle value in order is 5.

questions.prompt: Which daily figure of 3, 5, 5, 8 and 14 appears most often?
questions.hint: 5 appears most often.

questions.prompt: What gap separates the busiest and quietest of those five days?
questions.hint: 14 minus 3 is 11.

questions.prompt: What is the median of 2, 4, 6 and 10?
questions.hint: With an even number of values, take the mean of the two middle values: 4 and 6.

options.text: The data will be sorted incorrectly by the chart

questions.hint: A truncated axis exaggerates differences.

items.title: Handling information securely in everyday situations (Level 3)
items.source: Official Secrets Act 1989; Government Security Classifications; HMG Security Policy Framework
items.body: Security depends on everyday habits. The Official Secrets Act 1989 applies to Crown servants, including civil servants, and to government contractors. It makes it a criminal offence to disclose certain official information without authority, and civil servants may be asked to sign a declaration. These duties continue after you leave government service. Visitors should be signed in, wear a visitor pass and be escorted. Wear your own pass visibly, and report it quickly if it is lost. Do not hold a secure door open for people you do not know, because this is called tailgating, and politely ask them to use their own pass. When you work away from the office, use a department-approved device, keep your screen out of sight of others and use a VPN or other approved secure connection rather than open public Wi-Fi. Do not hold phone calls about sensitive matters in public places. Use removable media such as USB sticks only if they are approved and encrypted. Do not post information about your work on social media unless it is already public. Keep papers locked away when not in use. Report anything unusual, such as a lost pass, an unlocked cabinet or an unknown person in a secure area. You do not have to be sure that it is a problem. Early reporting stops small incidents becoming large ones.

items.title: UK GDPR in the workplace (Level 3)
items.body: Data protection affects how you do your job every day. You must only access personal data when you have a work reason. Looking up the record of a neighbour, relative or celebrity out of curiosity is not allowed, and knowingly obtaining or disclosing personal data without proper authority can be a criminal offence under the Data Protection Act 2018. Where consent is the lawful basis, it must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous. A pre-ticked box does not count. A data protection officer (DPO) advises the organisation and monitors compliance, and public authorities must have one. A data protection impact assessment (DPIA) is carried out before new processing that is likely to create a high risk to people, such as a new system holding sensitive data. A retention schedule sets out how long different records are kept and when they are destroyed. A controller decides why and how data is used. A processor handles data on the controller's behalf and must follow its instructions. When someone makes a subject access request, you should confirm their identity, find the data and reply within one month. Before sharing personal data with another organisation, check there is a lawful basis and, where appropriate, a written data sharing agreement. Only share what is needed.

options.text: It is acceptable if they have a valid security pass

questions.hint: Accessing personal data without a work reason breaks the law.

items.title: Passwords, ransomware and reporting a breach (Level 3)
items.source: NCSC guidance; ICO guidance on personal data breaches
items.body: Long passwords are harder to crack than short complicated ones. The NCSC recommends three random words, because length makes guessing by computers much harder and the password is still easy to remember. A password manager stores strong, unique passwords behind one master password. Always turn on multi-factor authentication where it is offered. Ransomware is malicious software that locks or encrypts files and demands payment. It often arrives through phishing emails. If you suspect it, disconnect from the network if you are told how, and tell your IT team immediately. A personal data breach includes emailing a spreadsheet to the wrong person, losing a laptop, a hacker accessing records and an employee looking at records they should not. When a breach happens, contain it first, for example by recalling a message or locking an account. Then report it to your manager and the data protection team straight away. The organisation must tell the ICO within 72 hours of becoming aware, unless the breach is unlikely to result in a risk to people's rights and freedoms. If there is a high risk to individuals, they must be told without undue delay. All breaches must be recorded internally, even if they are not reported to the ICO. A report should say what happened, when, whose data was involved and what has been done. Do not delete evidence or try to fix it quietly.

questions.hint: Length and memorability make this a strong approach.
